questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Kingdoms after the Mauryas' refers to.
questions.a: After the Mauryas, the subcontinent was reorganised into many kingdoms: Shaka and Kushana rulers from Central Asia, Satavahanas in the Deccan, and others who adopted Indian ways even as they arrived.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Kingdoms after the Mauryas'.
questions.a: Political break-up did not mean cultural break: new rulers settled in and joined the civilisation they entered.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Kingdoms after the Mauryas' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Trade Routes: Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha' refers to.
questions.a: Highways reorganised commerce: the Uttarapatha ran across the north, the Dakshinapatha pierced the Deccan to the southern ports, and both carried goods between land and sea routes to Rome and Southeast Asia.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Trade Routes: Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha'.
questions.a: Roads are arteries of civilisation: along the routes moved cloth, spices, coins, monks and ideas.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Trade Routes: Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Routes and trade (source: gees106.txt, Routes and trade)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'A Living Tradition of Change' refers to.
questions.a: The chapter opens with the thought that by a continuous living tradition and vital power of rejuvenescence, this land readjusted itself through unnumbered transformations; each new wave was absorbed and made Indian.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'A Living Tradition of Change'.
questions.a: India's strength is renewal: change after change left the civilisation itself alive and growing.

questions.q: Under which section is 'A Living Tradition of Change' taught, and from which source text?

concepts.title: Legacy of the Age of Reorganisation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Legacy of the Age of Reorganisation' refers to.
questions.a: The age left a legacy of devotional religion, Gandhara and Mathura art, Sanskrit literature and science, coinage and trade networks that later ages, including the Guptas, built upon.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Legacy of the Age of Reorganisation'.
questions.a: What looks like a pause between empires is a workshop: the reorganisation age forged the tools of the golden age to come.
